16-001.r: Prophet Hazrat Muhammad → born c. 570 A.D. in Mecca (Saudi Arabia); died 632 A.D.

16-003.r: 'Hindu' came from foreigners' pronunciation of Sindhu (Indus); book's answer: Arabs, but its explanation says Persians/Iranians first used it. Iranians said Hindustan; Greeks said India.
16-003.c: The explanation says the Persians (Iranians) first used 'Hindu'; they are not among the options, so the book picks (d) the Arabs. The Greeks said 'India'.

16-004.r: First successful Muslim invasion → Muhammad-bin-Qasim in Sindh, 712 A.D., defeating King Dahir; so 'None of these'. V.D. Mahajan dates it 711.
16-004.c: Key 'None of these' is debatable: the explanation notes V.D. Mahajan gives 711 A.D., which is an option.

16-006.r: First (successful) Muslim invader of India → Muhammad-bin-Qasim, early 8th century; Arab rule never spread east of Sindh and Multan.

16-007.r: First Muslim invaders of India → the Arabs under Muhammad-bin-Qasim, Sindh, 712 A.D.; ousted Raja Dahir (capital Arod, near Karachi).
16-007.t: Don't pick Ghaznavids or Ghurids; Turks came about three centuries after the Arabs.

16-008.r: Muhammad-bin-Qasim → an Arab (born c. 695 A.D.); nephew and son-in-law of Al Hajjaj of Iraq; sent to Sindh by Caliph al-Walid at seventeen.

16-009.r: Chachnama: Arod was capital of the Indus country (6th-7th century); Arabic history of Sindh, named after Raja Chach, father of Dahir.

16-010.r: Chachnama (Arabic; Sindh history 680-718 A.D.) → Persian translation by Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi; English by Mirza Kalich Beg (1900).

16-011.r: Founder of the Ghaznavid dynasty → Alptigin, a Turkish slave-governor of the Samanids, with capital at Ghazni.
16-011.t: Don't confuse founder Alptigin with Sebuktigin (his successor line) or Mahmud (the famous raider).

16-012.r: A true: Mahmud of Ghazni raided India 17 times (1000-1027 A.D.). R false: he sought wealth, not a permanent Muslim empire.
16-012.h: Mahmud = money, not territory; 17 raids, no rule.

16-013.r: Chandela king not defeated by Mahmud Ghaznavi → Vidyadhar, who repulsed him (1019-20 A.D.); Chandela capital Khajuraho, later Mahoba.

16-015.r: Mahmud of Ghazni's court historian → Utbi (Kitab-ul-Yamini/Tarikh-i-Yamini); Firdausi → Shahnama ('Homer of the East'); Alberuni → Tahqiq-i-Hind.

16-016.r: Shahnama → Firdausi (not Firishta), court poet of Mahmud of Ghazni, 'Homer of the East'; Firishta wrote Tarikh-i-Firishta.
16-016.t: Don't confuse Firdausi (Shahnama, Ghazni) with Firishta (Tarikh-i-Firishta, Deccan).
16-016.c: No answer printed; question wrongly names Farista as Shahnama's author; book says (b) Mahmud Ghaznavi is meant.

16-018.r: First Muslim to study the Puranas → Al-Biruni; learnt Sanskrit; interested in astronomy, geography, medicine, maths, religion.

16-019.r: Historian who came with Mahmud of Ghazni → Al-Beruni (11th century A.D.); translated Patanjali's Yoga-Sutra into Arabic; main work Tahqiq-i-Hind.

16-022.r: Wrong about Alberuni: 'secular author' (he gave no sympathetic word on Mahmud's Somnath raid, 1025/1026). He was a Sanskrit scholar, trigonometry expert; born 973 A.D., Khwarizm.

16-023.r: Somnath temple rebuilt after Mahmud Ghazni's raid (1025/26 AD) → Bhimadeva I, ruler at the time of the attack.

16-024.r: Somnath (Gujarat, Arabian Sea): one of 12 Jyotirlingas; described by Al-Biruni. Present temple's Pran Pratishtha → President Rajendra Prasad, not S. Radhakrishnan.

16-025.r: Silver coins with Sanskrit legend → Mahmud of Ghazni (Arabic and Sanskrit inscriptions, struck in India).

16-026.r: Conqueror of North India in 1192 → Shihabuddin Muhammad Ghori; Multan 1175, Gujarat 1178, lost First Tarain 1191, won Second Tarain 1192.

16-027.r: First to defeat Muhammad Ghori → Mularaja II (Bhimadev II) of Gujarat, with regent mother Naika Devi; Ghori never again came via Gujarat.

16-028.r: Ghori defeated Jayachandra of Kannauj → Battle of Chandawar (1194 A.D.), on the Yamuna in modern Firozabad district, near Agra.
16-028.t: Don't confuse with Tarain 1191/1192, which were against Prithviraj Chauhan.

16-031.r: Battle that founded Muslim domination → Second Battle of Tarain (1192 AD); Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan.

16-032.r: Order: Mahmud Ghaznavi (1000-1027) → Muhammad Ghori (1175-1205) → Genghis Khan (1221, chasing Jalaluddin) → Taimur (1398).

16-033.r: Coins bearing Goddess Lakshmi → Muhammad Ghori.

16-034.r: First Iqta in India → Qutbuddin Aybak, made in charge of Indian lands (1192 A.D.) and of Kuhram and Samana by Muhammad Ghori.

16-035.r: Ghori's slave who conquered Bihar and Bengal → Bakhtiyar Khalji (1193-1203 in Bihar); destroyed Nalanda and Vikramshila, took Odantpur; Lakshman Sen fled Bengal.

16-039.r: A and R true, R explains A: Turkish invasions succeeded because North India lacked political unity (many small warring kingdoms).

16-040.r: A and R true, R explains A: Turks (Mahmud, Ghori) succeeded as North India was split into small states; Ghori's conquest led to the Delhi Sultanate.

17-001.r: Founder of the Slave dynasty → Qutbuddin Aybak (1206 A.D.); dynasty ruled 1206-1290, first of five Sultanate dynasties.

17-002.r: First Slave dynasty ruler → Qutbuddin Aybak (1206-1210 A.D.), capital Lahore; as a boy sold to Qazi Fakhruddin of Nishapur.

17-003.r: 'Lakh Baksh' (for generosity) → Qutbuddin Aybak; began Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (Delhi), Adhai Din ka Jhonpra mosque (Ajmer) and the Qutub Minar.

17-006.r: Qutb Minar: begun by Aybak, completed by Iltutmish; lightning-damaged top rebuilt by Firuz Shah Tughluq (fourth floor restored, fifth added). Ghiyasuddin Tughluq had no role.

17-008.r: Qutbuddin Aybak's capital → Lahore; Taj-ud-Din Yalduz (Governor of Kirman) took Ghazni after Ghori's death (1206 A.D.).
17-008.t: Delhi became capital only under Iltutmish.

17-009.r: Aybak died 1210 A.D. after falling from his horse while playing Chaugan (polo); buried at Lahore near Anarkali Bazaar.

17-010.r: Made Delhi the Sultanate capital → Iltutmish (1211-36 AD), real founder of Delhi Sultanate; first regular Arabic silver (175 grain) and copper coins.

17-012.r: Capital under Iltutmish → Delhi; he was the first Sultan to shift the capital (from Lahore to Delhi).

17-014.r: First legally independent Sultan of Delhi → Iltutmish; Caliph Al-Muntasir Billah of Baghdad gave him investiture and title 'Sultan-i-Azam' (1229 A.D.).

17-015.r: Ruler whose empire became part of Dar-ul-Islam → Iltutmish, after the Caliph of Baghdad sent him khillat (1229 A.D.).

17-016.r: 'Slave of a slave' → Iltutmish: slave (and son-in-law) of Qutbuddin Aybak, who was himself Muhammad Ghori's slave.

17-017.r: Not Iltutmish's rival → Malik Altunia. Rivals: Tajuddin Yalduz (Ghazni), Nasiruddin Qabacha (Sindh), Ali Mardan (Lakhnauti); Iltutmish took power after Aram Shah.

17-018.r: First woman ruler of medieval India → Raziyya Sultan (1236-1240 A.D.), only woman on the Delhi Sultanate throne.
17-018.t: Don't pick Chand Bibi, Durgavati or Noorjahan; they came later and never ruled Delhi.

17-019.r: Genghis Khan reached the Indus (NW frontier) in Iltutmish's reign, chasing Khwarizm prince Jalaluddin Mengubirni; Iltutmish wisely refused him asylum.

17-023.r: Original name of Changez (Genghis) Khan → Temujin (Temuchin).

17-024.r: Only 1 correct: Chengiz Khan reached the Indus under Iltutmish. Wrong: Taimur's conquests began 1370, after Muhammad bin Tughluq (1325-1351); Deva Raya II received Abdur Razzaq.

17-025.r: Iltutmish's first Subedar of Bihar → Malik Jani, after defeating Iwaz (Ghiyasuddin) near Teliyagarhi in 1225 A.D.

17-026.r: Raziyya dethroned by the Turkish nobles, led by Malik Altunia, governor of Bhatinda.

17-027.r: Balban's full name → Ghiyasuddin Balban; ninth Mamluk Sultan; earlier Wazir and heir of Nasiruddin Mahmud.

17-028.r: 'Blood and iron' policy → Balban; Sultan as God's representative (Niyabat-i-Khudai), next only to the Prophet; autocratic, divine-right kingship.

17-030.r: A and R true, R not the explanation: Balban (1266-1287 A.D.) centralised all power as a divine right; separately built forts in the north-west against Mongols.

17-032.r: Balban's grand title → Zil-e-Ilahi ('Shadow of God'); king as Niyabat-e-Khudai.
17-032.t: Don't confuse with Din-e-Ilahi (Akbar's faith) or Tuti-e-Hind (Amir Khusrau).

17-033.r: First Muslim ruler with a 'theory of kingship' like divine right → Balban: Sultan is God's representative, next to the Paigambar.

17-034.r: Persian festival Nawruz introduced in India → Balban; also brought Iranian court customs Sijada (prostration) and Paibos (kissing feet).

17-036.r: Not true of Balban: Iqtadari system (Iltutmish's). True: Niyabat-e-Khudai theory, ended Turkan-e-Chahalgani, crushed Bengal revolt (Tughril, 1279); first used 'Zillillah'.

17-038.r: 'Helper of a Caliph' in the Garhmukteshwar mosque inscription → Balban.

17-039.r: Tughril Khan's revolt (Bengal) → Balban's reign; sparked by Amin Khan's posting in Bengal; Tughril fled Balban's Bengal campaign.

18-001.r: Sultan who planned a new religion → Alauddin Khalji; dropped it on Kotwal Ala-ul-Mulk's advice; took title Sikandar-i-Sani (second Alexander) on coins.

18-003.r: Titles Yamin-ul-Khilafat and Nasir-e-Amir-ul-Mominin → Alauddin Khalji (also 'Sikandar Sani' on coins).

18-004.r: Barani on a king 'independent of rulers and orders of Shariat' → Alauddin Khalji.

18-005.r: Alauddin's commander killed fighting the Mongols → Zafar Khan (original name Malik Hizabruddin).

18-006.r: Padmini (Chittor) → wife of Rana Ratan Singh; story told in Padmavat by Malik Muhammad Jayasi (1540 AD).

18-007.r: 'Hazar-Dinari' → Malik Kafur, obtained by Alauddin Khalji during the Gujarat conquest.

18-008.r: Malik Kafur ('Hazar Dinari', once bought for a thousand dinars) → taken by Nusrat Khan in the Gujarat campaign and presented to Alauddin Khalji.
18-008.c: Explanation says Nusrat Khan seized Kafur by force; it was his earlier master who bought him, so 'bought by Nusrat Khan' is loose.

18-009.r: A true: Alauddin's Deccan expeditions were for wealth. R false: he did not want to annex the Deccan states (K.S. Lal).

18-010.r: Devgiri ruler at Alauddin's invasion → Ramchandra Dev (1296 A.D.); he stopped Ellichpur tribute, so Malik Kafur attacked Devgiri in 1307.

18-011.r: Alauddin's foes: Ranthambore → Hamirdeva; Chittor → Rana Ratan Singh; Devagiri → Raja Rai Ramchandra; Gujarat → Karnadeva.

18-012.r: Alauddin's conquests in order: Gujarat (1299) → Ranthambor (1301) → Chittor (1303) → Warangal (1310).
18-012.h: Odd years climb: 1299, 1301, 1303, then jump to 1310.

18-013.r: Alauddin's campaigns in order: Jaisalmer (1299) → Ranthambore (1301) → Chittor (1303) → Warangal of the Kakatiyas (1309-1310).

18-014.r: Map route of the southern campaign → Malik Kafur ('Hazar-Dinari'), Alauddin's commander, found during the Gujarat conquest.

18-015.r: Khalisa (crown) land expanded greatly → Alauddin Khalji, who took back Milk (state-gifted), Idrar (pension) and Waqf (charity) lands.

18-016.r: Land revenue raised to one-half of produce → Alauddin Khalji (by measurement) and Muhammad-bin-Tughluq (Doab, by estimate); book accepts both.

18-018.r: Half the crop as revenue after measuring land → Alauddin Khalji; Muhammad-bin-Tughluq's half-share in the Doab was based on expected yield.

18-019.r: Alauddin: collected revenue by measuring land (I) and curbed provincial governors (III); measurement only around Delhi, not the whole empire (II false).

18-020.r: A true: Alauddin introduced price control in Delhi (Shehna Malik Kabool). R false: aim was to support a vast army against Mongols, not low wages to artisans.

18-022.r: Strict price/market control → Alauddin Khalji; first Sultan to pay army in cash; Barani: normal wages would empty treasury in 5-6 years.

18-024.r: Alauddin's market price control → highly successful (book); aimed to maintain a vast standing army; separate markets in Delhi (grain mandi, cloth and groceries).

18-025.r: Medieval 'Public Distribution System' → started by Alauddin Khalji (Sultanate period).

18-027.r: First 'Ghari' (house) tax → Alauddin Khalji; also a grazing tax on milch animals.

18-028.r: Delhi Sultanate–Mongol boundary after 1306 A.D. → Ravi; Malik Kafur and Ghazi Malik stopped Kabak's Mongols there.

18-029.r: Only 2 correct: Under Alauddin, Mongol Qutlugh Khwaja besieged Delhi. Wrong: first Mongol attack was under Iltutmish; Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq repelled Tarmashirin, held Kalanaur and Peshawar.

18-030.r: Sultan who raised a special big army to guard the empire's borders → Alauddin Khalji, with a strong central government.

18-031.r: Wrong pair: Warangal–Ramchandra Dev; Ramchandra Dev ruled Devgiri (later his son Shankar Dev). Correct: Devgiri–Shankar Dev, Hoysala–Veer Ballal, Madura–Veer Pandya.

18-032.r: No Sultan in the options opposed the Caliph; Iltutmish got Caliph's recognition; Alauddin, Balban, Muhammad-bin-Tughluq were practically independent but never opposed him.

18-033.r: Delhi ruler who declared himself Khalifa → Qutbuddin Mubarak Khalji (title Al-Imam, Khilafatullah); the only one to do so.

18-034.r: Kakatiya army defeated Alauddin's army at Warangal in 1303 (led by Fakhruddin Juna and Malik Chhajju); Kakatiya king Prataprudradev II.

19-001.r: Alauddin's general who founded the Tughluq dynasty → Ghazi Malik (Ghiyasuddin Tughluq); governor of Multan and Depalpur; beat Mongols 29 times (Ibn Battuta).

19-003.r: First 14th-century ruler credited with digging irrigation canals → Ghiyasuddin Tughluq; land revenue fixed at 1/10 or 1/11; restored rights of Khuts and Muqaddams.

19-004.r: Longest-ruling Sultanate dynasty (of these) → Tughluq (1320-1412); Slave 1206-1290, Khalji 1290-1320, Lodi 1451-1526.

19-005.r: Most learned Delhi Sultan, versed in astronomy, mathematics and medicine → Muhammad-bin-Tughluq (1325-1351 AD).

19-006.r: New department Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi (Diwan-i-Kohi) for agriculture → Muhammad-bin-Tughluq; a 30 × 30 karoh tract farmed with crop rotation.

19-007.r: Separate agriculture department 'Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi' with planned rotation of crops → Muhammad Tughlaq.
19-007.t: Don't confuse Diwan-i-Kohi (Muhammad Tughlaq, agriculture) with Diwan-i-Khairat (Firuz, charity).

19-010.r: Capital shifted from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devgiri) → Muhammad-bin-Tughluq; Barani: Devgiri central to the empire; Ibn Battuta: to punish Delhi's rude letter-writers.
19-010.h: Devgiri → Qutbabad (Mubarak Khalji) → Daulatabad (Muhammad Tughluq), per K.A. Nizami.

19-012.r: First token currency in India → Muhammad-bin-Tughluq, due to lack of silver in the treasury (Barani); idea earlier tried in Iran under Gaykhatu.

19-014.r: A true: Muhammad-bin-Tughluq issued a gold coin Ibn Battuta called Dinar. R false: token currency was copper/bronze, not gold, and not for West Asian trade.

19-015.r: A and R true, R explains A: token currency failed as the state did not control minting (forgery). Barani's five schemes: Doab tax, Devgiri capital, token currency, Khurasan, Qarachil.

19-016.r: Ibn Battuta (Moroccan, 1304-1377) → came under Muhammad-bin-Tughluq (1333-1342); made Qazi of Delhi; envoy to China 1342; wrote Kitab-ul-Rihla.

19-019.r: Detailed account of the Sultanate postal system → Ibn Battuta (from Tangier, Morocco), in Kitab-ul-Rihla.

19-020.r: Yousuf Shah Chak, last Muslim ruler of Kashmir valley, exiled to Bihar by Akbar → died 1592 AD, buried at Nalanda.

19-021.r: First Delhi Sultan to join public Holi celebrations → Muhammad-bin-Tughluq.

19-022.r: 'The king was freed from his people and they from their king' → Badayuni on Muhammad-bin-Tughluq's death (20 March 1351, near Thatta, chasing rebel Taghi).

19-023.r: Badayuni's remark 'the king was freed from his people and they from their king' (in Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh) → on Muhammad-bin-Tughluq's death.

19-024.r: Sultan who opened an employment office (employment exchange) for the jobless → Firuz Shah Tughluq.

19-026.r: Diwan-i-Khairat (charity department: poor Muslims, orphans, widows, marriages of poor girls) → Firuz Tughluq.

19-027.r: Sultan with the most slaves → Firuz Tughluq (about one lakh eighty thousand); separate department Diwan-i-Bandgan; slaves paid 10 to 100 Tankas.

19-028.r: Correct: Firuz Tughluq set up a slave department (Diwan-i-Bandgan). Wrong: Diwan-i-Arz was Balban's (book); horse branding was Alauddin's; Muhammad-bin-Tughluq succeeded by cousin Firuz.

19-029.r: Public Works Department → Firuz Shah Tughluq; founded 200 new cities incl. Fatehabad, Hisar, Firozpur, Jaunpur, Firozabad.

19-030.r: Biggest canal network → Firuz Shah Tughluq (e.g. Yamuna to Hisar 150 miles, Sutlej to Ghaggar 96 miles); first to levy Haqq-i-Sharb (irrigation tax).
19-030.h: Firuz = Fountains and canals; Haqq-i-Sharb, sharb = water.

19-033.r: Sultan who levied Jizya on Brahmins → Firuz Tughlaq; Jizya = religious tax on non-Muslims.

19-034.r: Measures to improve fruit quality → Firuz Tughluq; planted 1200 new orchards near Delhi, restored 30 of Alauddin's gardens.

19-035.r: Brought two Ashoka pillars to Delhi from Topra (Yamunanagar, Haryana) and Meerut → Firuz Shah Tughluq; Topra pillar set up at his Firozabad palace.

19-037.r: Translation Department so Hindus and Muslims could understand each other → Firuz Tughluq; Sanskrit texts put into Persian.

19-038.r: 300 Sanskrit books seized at Nagarkot (Jwalamukhi temple) by Firuz Tughlaq → translated into Persian by Azizuddin Khan.

19-039.r: First Indian ruler to fund Haj from the state treasury → Firuz Tughluq; also Dar-ul-Shafa (free hospital) and Diwan-i-Khairat.

19-041.r: Last Tughluq ruler → Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah (1394-1412 A.D.); Khwaja Jahan made Jaunpur independent; rival Nusrat Shah ruled from Firozabad.

19-042.r: Timur invaded India in 1398 A.D. during Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah's reign (1394-1412); left Khizr Khan as subedar of Multan, Depalpur and Lahore.
19-042.c: No answer printed; none of the options is correct (the ruler was Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah).

19-044.r: Dynasty after Timur's invasion (1398) → Sayyid, founded 1414 AD by Khizr Khan, Timur's subedar of Lahore; Tughluqs ended 1412.

19-045.r: Order: Rukn-ud-din (1236 A.D.) → Mubarak Khan Khalji (1316-1320) → Firuz Shah Tughluq (1351-1388) → Alam Shah (1445-1451).

20-001.r: Afghan-origin Sultanate dynasty → Lodi (1451-1526 A.D.), last Delhi Sultanate dynasty; ended when Babur beat Ibrahim Lodi at First Panipat (1526).

20-002.r: Lodi order: Bahlul Lodi (1451-1489, founder) → Sikandar Lodi (1489-1517) → Ibrahim Lodi (1517-1526).
20-002.h: B-S-I: Bahlul built, Sikandar strengthened, Ibrahim lost.

20-003.r: Map → Bahlul Lodi's kingdom; place 'A' = Jaunpur, then called 'Shiraz-i-Hind'.

20-004.r: Rana Sanga defeated Ibrahim Lodi → Battle of Khatoli (1518 A.D.).
20-004.t: Don't confuse with Khanua, where Babur defeated Sanga.

20-005.r: Agra founded (1504 A.D.) and made capital → Sikandar Lodi (Nizam Khan, Bahlul's son; throne 1489); wrote poems as 'Gulrukhi'.

20-010.r: Sultan who abolished several grain taxes → Sikandar Lodi; introduced Gaz-i-Sikandari for land measurement, later used by Sher Shah and Akbar.

20-011.h: Sultanate: 'Sab Khana Tum Sab Lo' = Slave, Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid, Lodi.

20-012.r: Not from the Slave dynasty → Ibrahim Lodi (Lodi); Qutbuddin Aibak (1206-10), Iltutmish (1211-36), Balban (1266-86) were.

21-001.r: Vijayanagara founded by Harihara and Bukka in 1336 (Sangama dynasty, named after their father); once feudatories of the Kakatiyas of Warangal.

21-003.r: Vijayanagara Empire established → 1336 A.D. by Harihara I and his brother Bukka I, former Kakatiya officials.
21-003.t: Don't confuse 1336 with 1236 or 1436; same year Harihara-Bukka began.

21-004.r: Founders of Vijayanagara (1336 A.D., banks of the Tungabhadra) → brothers Harihara and Bukka.

21-007.r: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva → Vijayanagara dynasties: Sangama (1336-1485), Saluva (1485-1505), Tuluva (1505-1570), Aravidu (1570-1672).
21-007.h: Vijayanagara dynasties in order: S-S-T-A, 'Sangama Saluva Tuluva Aravidu'.

21-008.r: Harihara I → founded a city on the south bank of the Tungabhadra (Krishna tributary), ruling as agent of a deity owning all land south of the Krishna.

21-009.r: Madhura Vijayam → Ganga Devi, wife of Kumara Kampana (son of Bukka I), on his conquest of Madurai (1365-1370).

21-010.r: First Vijayanagara ruler to take Goa from the Bahmanis → Harihara II (king after 1377 A.D.); also won Belgaum; title Maharajadhiraja.

21-011.r: Dam on the Tungabhadra (c. 1410 AD) and a 24 km canal-cum-aqueduct to the capital → Devaraya I.

21-012.r: All four true: Narasimha Saluva ended Sangama rule (1485 AD); Vira Narasimha deposed the last Saluva, founded Tuluva; then brother Krishnadeva Raya; then Achyuta Deva Raya.

21-013.r: Battle of Golconda → Krishnadeva Raya vs Quli Qutb Shah, founder of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda.

21-014.r: Permission to the Portuguese to build a fort at Bhatkal → Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva, 1509-1529 AD), at Albuquerque's request; bought guns and Arabian horses from them.

21-015.r: Ashtadiggajas → eight Telugu poets in Krishnadeva Raya's court; his reign = golden age of Telugu literature; his title 'Andhra Bhoja'; Peddana foremost.
21-015.h: Ashta (eight) + diggaja (elephants holding up the directions) = eight pillars of his court.

21-019.r: City founded by Krishnadeva Raya → Nagalapura (Nagalapuram), in honour of his mother; also credited with Hazara Rama and Vitthala temples.

21-020.r: True: Krishnadevaraya wrote Amuktamalyada; called Andhra Bhoj. False: Allasani Peddana was a poet of Telugu and Sanskrit, not Sanskrit and Tamil.

21-021.r: Suburban township Nagalapuram near Vijayanagara → Krishnadevaraya, named after his mother Nagala Devi.

21-022.r: Hazara Rama temple, Vijayanagara → built in Krishnadeva Raya's reign.

21-023.r: 'Andhra Kavita Pitamah' → Allasani Peddana, greatest of the Ashtadiggajas; Krishnadeva Raya himself wrote the Telugu epic Amuktamalyada.

21-024.r: Mallanarya's Bhava Chinta Ratna and Veerasaivamrita (Shaiva works, court of Krishnadeva Raya, 1509–1529 AD) → written in Kannada.
21-024.t: Not Telugu: the Ashtadiggajas wrote Telugu, but Mallanarya wrote Kannada.

21-025.r: Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq → visited Vijayanagara under Devaraya II (1422-46 AD), Sangama dynasty.
21-025.t: Don't mix: Nicolo Conti came under Deva Raya I; Abdur Razzaq under Deva Raya II.

21-028.r: Nicolo Conti → Italian traveller who visited Vijayanagara in Deva Raya I's time.

21-029.r: Nuniz (Portuguese, under Achyuta Deva Raya): Vijayanagara women were wrestlers, astrologers, accountants and soothsayers (all four); also dancers, servants, palanquin bearers.

21-030.r: Telugu translators → Nannaya and Tikkana; with Yerrapragada they form the Kavi Traya, who rendered the Mahabharata into Telugu (11th-14th century).

21-031.r: Sayana, Vedic commentator → patronised by Vijayanagara rulers; he and brother Madhav Vidyaranya inspired the empire's founding.

21-033.r: Enthroned 500 years before 2008 → Krishnadeva Raya (ruled 1509-1529 AD), greatest Vijayanagara emperor.
21-033.c: Book calls the question erroneous (Harihara I and Kulottunga I also passed 500 years) and picks (b) as nearest.

21-034.r: Battle of Talikota (1565 A.D.) → Vijayanagara defeated by Deccan Sultanates Bijapur, Bidar, Ahmadnagar, Golconda (Berar not included).
